responses: My final position is an unwavering commitment to the "One System" allocation of **30% Education, 22% Healthcare, 16% Infrastructure, 15% Economic Development, and 15% Green Spaces**, as this is the only strategy capable of preventing Greenfield from becoming a "Ghost Town" of empty streets and failing institutions. I believe that traditional notions of "fairness," which would spread the $10 million grant thinly across all five areas, are actually a form of negligence that guarantees every sector fails because none receive the critical mass needed to function; instead, we must treat our community as a living organism requiring immediate triage, where the bleeding in our classrooms and the crisis in our healthcare system are addressed first to stabilize the engine of our town. By prioritizing the retention of teachers, the mental and physical well-being of families, and the digital and economic infrastructure that connects us to the future, we are not just balancing a budget but investing in the very survival of our community, ensuring that our children have a reason to stay and our neighbors have a reason to thrive.

I strongly recommend adopting the **30/22/16/15/15** allocation strategy, prioritizing Education and Healthcare as the non-negotiable foundation for Greenfield's survival, because the data clearly indicates that our community is facing a "bleeding" crisis of teacher turnover and family outmigration that a "fair" equal split would only exacerbate. By directing 30% to Education, we stop the immediate loss of talent and signal to families that their children's future is secure here, while the 22% investment in Healthcare ensures the physical and mental well-being of the workforce needed to sustain that growth. The remaining funds—16% for modern Infrastructure (specifically broadband and transit), 15% for Economic Development to create local jobs, and 15% for Green Spaces to foster community pride—act as the essential connective tissue that turns a school district into a thriving ecosystem. Any attempt to dilute these critical investments in favor of superficial "fairness" risks creating a "Ghost Town" with pristine roads but no residents; therefore, we must treat this not as a budget exercise, but as a triage protocol where concentrating resources on the vital organs of our community is the only path to a living, breathing future.

If I were explaining our decision to a neighbor who wasn't in the room, I would tell them that we made the hardest but most necessary choice to save Greenfield from becoming a "ghost town" of empty streets and closed schools. Instead of spreading our $10 million grant thinly across all five areas to look "fair," we adopted a "One System" strategy that prioritizes the people who make our community alive: we allocated 30% to Education to stop the bleeding of teachers and students, 22% to Healthcare to ensure our families are well enough to thrive, and the remaining funds to Infrastructure, Economic Development, and Green Spaces to create a connected, employable, and soulful home. We realized that fixing potholes or building pretty parks means nothing if our schools are failing and our young people are forced to leave; by concentrating our resources on the engine of our community first, we aren't just balancing a budget, we are choosing life over stagnation and ensuring that Greenfield remains a place where families can build a future rather than just a place they pass through.

My final position is an unwavering commitment to the "One System" allocation of **30% Education, 22% Healthcare, 16% Infrastructure, 15% Economic Development, and 15% Green Spaces**, as this is the only strategy that addresses Greenfield's critical risk of becoming a "Ghost Town." The data clearly shows that our schools are failing to retain families and our teachers are burning out, making the 30% investment in Education the non-negotiable engine of our survival, while the 22% for Healthcare ensures our population is healthy enough to build and learn. This allocation is not merely a budget but a biological necessity for a living community, ensuring that our roads lead to a thriving town, our parks are filled with life, and our young people have a reason to stay and call Greenfield home.
